conceptTag: Test an idea in one week with $500
readerTitle: One week, $500: should Maya's shop start restocking offices?
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (철물·생활용품 매장이 사무실 정기 보충 서비스를 시험) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 아이디어 시험은 무엇을 만들까가 아니라, 사업을 무너뜨릴 질문 하나에 가장 싸게 실제 행동으로 답하는 일이다.
misconception: 제대로 시험하려면 먼저 그럴듯하게 갖춰야 한다. 관심 있다는 말이 많으면 수요가 확인된 것이다.

sources.text: 모든 인물, 사업, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시
유닛 CUS-04의 개념(가장 위험한 가정, 가짜 문 테스트, 선판매, 손으로 먼저 해보기, 만들기·측정·학습)을 하나의 이야기로 엮은 시뮬레이션

factChecks.note: 선판매 계산: 3곳 × 첫 달 $150 = $450. 물품 원가 곳당 $90($270 ÷ 3)이므로 곳당 남는 돈 $60, 이 돈으로 방문 시간(약 40분)을 감당해야 함.
퍼널 수치: 방문 30곳 → 관심 9곳 → 결제 3곳. 9곳에서 3곳으로 3분의 2 감소. 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: One week, $500: should Maya's shop start restocking offices?
body: Maya runs a hardware and cleaning-supply shop. On weekdays, office managers rush in for paper towels, soap and coffee filters, usually because they ran out.
Her idea: a monthly service where she checks each office's supply cupboard and refills it. Before she leases a van, she gives herself one week and $500 to find out if it works. You make her calls.

image.label: Shop owner looking at an empty office supply cupboard
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 생활용품 매장 주인이 사무실의 텅 빈 비품장(휴지, 세제, 커피 필터 자리만 남음)을 들여다보는 장면. 옆에 "1 week · $500"이라 적힌 메모. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya test first?
body: She has dozens of open questions and time to answer only a few well.

options.text: Whether her suppliers will give her bulk prices
options.feedback: Useful, and three phone calls will answer it. But good prices won't save a service nobody signs up for.

options.text: Whether office managers will hand over their cupboard and pay a monthly fee
options.feedback: If this answer is no, nothing else matters. She aims the whole week at the question most likely to kill the idea.

options.text: Whether she can plan delivery routes efficiently
options.feedback: Routes matter only once there are customers. She'd spend the week solving a problem she may never have.

cards.title: Say you chose to test demand. How does she spend the money?

options.text: Buy $450 of stock and branded boxes so the service looks real
options.feedback: It looks professional, but almost all the money is gone before one customer has said yes.

options.text: Print a one-page offer with a clear price and walk into 30 nearby offices
options.feedback: For about $40 she shows a real offer to real buyers. The service doesn't exist yet, but their reaction does.

options.text: Email her customer list a survey asking if they'd use it
options.feedback: Nearly free, but it collects opinions. Saying "sounds useful" costs a busy manager nothing.

cards.softwareNote: A software founder does the same with a landing page showing a price and a "Start" button, before the product is built. Clicks on a real offer beat answers to a survey.

cards.title: Nine of 30 offices say they're interested. Now what?

options.text: Call it a success and sign the van lease
options.feedback: "Interested" is still a free answer. She'd commit thousands on the strength of polite nods.

options.text: Ask the nine to pay the first month, $150, now, with a full refund if she doesn't deliver
options.feedback: Money turns interest into evidence. The refund keeps the risk low for them, so a no really means no.

options.text: Offer the first month free to get them started
options.feedback: She'd get users quickly, but she'd learn nothing about whether anyone will pay $150.

cards.title: Three offices paid. How does she deliver?

options.text: Buy route-planning software and a used van
options.feedback: She'd build for a fleet when she has three customers, and spend money the test was meant to protect.

options.text: Pack orders from her own shelves, drive them herself, and time every task
options.feedback: It's slow and doesn't scale, which is fine. She sees exactly what the job involves and what it costs.

options.text: Hire a courier for the week
options.feedback: It saves her time, but she misses what happens at the cupboard: what ran out, who signs, how long it takes.

cards.callout: Say she chose B. Here's what the week showed.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders call this doing things that don't scale: running a "feature" by hand behind the scenes before writing the code.

cards.title: Interest is not the same as payment.
body: Two thirds of the "interested" offices disappeared when she asked for money. Three real customers are worth more than nine maybes.
Doing it by hand taught her something no survey would: each visit took about 40 minutes, far longer than she'd guessed. Her price may be too low.
cards.callout: She built little, measured behavior, and learned what to fix next.

cards.title: Where the $500 went.
body: The three prepaid months brought in **$450**. After $90 of stock each, Maya keeps $60 per office to pay for 40 minutes of her time.

breakdown.label: Stock
breakdown.detail: Supplies for three offices, at cost

breakdown.label: Unspent
breakdown.detail: Nothing went on a van or software

cards.softwareNote: The same math applies to a software test: what each paying user brings in, minus what serving them by hand actually costs.

cards.title: A good week is a start, not proof.
body: Three customers are not a market. They're nearby and may know Maya, which makes yes easier.

One week can't show the most important thing: whether they pay again next month. And the by-hand version is a test, not the business. At 40 minutes a visit, it can't grow without a change in price or method.
The right next step is another small test, not a big launch.

cards.title: Answer the question that could kill the idea, as cheaply as you can.
body: Each of Maya's calls used one idea from this unit:
list: **Day 2:** show a real offer before the product exists
**Day 4:** ask for money to turn interest into evidence
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down the one belief that would sink your next idea if it were wrong. Name the cheapest way to see a customer act on it this week.
